In [[mathematics]], a function <math>f</math> is '''weakly harmonic''' in a domain <math>D</math> if  
:<math>\int_D f\, \Delta g = 0</math>

for all <math>g</math> with [[compact support]] in <math>D</math> and continuous second derivatives, where &Delta; is the [[Laplacian]].<ref name="gilbarg">{{cite book |last1=Gilbarg |first1=David |last2=Trudinger |first2=Neil S. |title=Elliptic partial differential equations of second order |date=12 January 2001 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=9783540411604 |page=29 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eoiGTf4cmhwC |access-date=26 April 2023}}</ref> This is the same notion as a [[weak derivative]], however, a function can have a weak derivative and not be differentiable.  In this case, we have the somewhat surprising result that a function is weakly harmonic if and only if it is harmonic.  Thus weakly harmonic is actually equivalent to the seemingly stronger harmonic condition.
